item.title: Enough Already! Stop Trying to Prove You Were a Good Parent
item.description:
Forgiveness

Enough Already! Stop Trying to Prove You Were a Good Parent

Your adult child may never give you the verdict you keep hoping to hear.

Posted August 23, 2026

Key points
  • You can acknowledge your parenting mistakes without accepting responsibility for everything that followed.
  • Repeatedly defending, explaining, and even apologies keeps you and your adult child stuck in a courtroom.
  • The goal is not to win agreement about the past. Rather, it is to build a healthier relationship in the now.

I hear some version of this from my parent coaching fairly often: "Dr. Jeff, I just want her to understand that I did the best I could." What I then try to do is gently explore the painful question that often lurks underneath these parents' understandable concerns: to feel appreciated by their adult children. And that question is, "When will my adult child finally admit I wasn't such a bad parent?"

The sobering answer for many parents is that they may never hear enough words (or maybe even any words) of appreciation from their adult children. Or, as we dig deeper, many of these parents have heard some appreciation expressed in the past, but it has been overwritten by arguments or silence. Even if they once heard appreciation, parents still want to feel some sense of ongoing appreciation, and it is hard for them to accept not getting it.

Spending Way Too Many Years Trying to Win a Case That Has No Jury

The sad truth is that many parents become very intent on explaining things to their adult children, like how they worked too much, highlighting the lows of their marriage, or (and this goes over like a "Led Zeppelin") listing everything they did for their kids over the years. I understand why they feel defensive and compelled to do so, but these "proving ground" statements usually only create more distance with their adult children. Their hope is, "If I can just get my adult child to see the whole story, maybe we can finally move on." But sadly, the result is the relationship being hyper-focused on the "trial" of the parent.

There May Be Truth in What the Adult Children May Be Saying

In my book, You Ruined My Life Now You Owe Me—How to Stop Rescuing, Reduce Conflict, and Help Your Adult Child Move Forward, I further describe those parents who feel as though they are standing in a courtroom where the verdict has already been reached. In the minds of the struggling adult children, each present-day struggle (relationship problems, job problems, or low self-confidence) becomes another link to their parents' failings. But stay with me here: Is there some truth to what these adult children are saying?

Maybe, for example, you were too critical, or maybe your anxiety did often spill over to your kids. What I am saying is that you regret some things. Acknowledging those issues matters, but that is different from accepting a life sentence of blame being hurled at you.

A Healthier Way to Respond

One father I worked with apologized repeatedly to his son for being emotionally distant when he was young. And very few months later, the son's accusations of emotional neglect resurfaced. One dramatic evening, when the father tried one more time to apologize, the son passively aggressively sang Harry Chapin's song, Cat's In The Cradle (about a father who worked too much and his grown son did the same and, when grown, did not have time for his father). As a target of our coaching work, the father stopped trying to produce the perfect apology. Instead, he said something like, "I know I hurt you in ways I wish I hadn't. And I also want to have a relationship with you that isn't only about what happened years ago."

The Takeaway

It is healthy for you as a parent to apologize when an apology is merited. But sometimes moving forward begins when you stop trying to win a case in the court of family history.

item.title: Reading Fiction Can Boost Your Emotional Intelligence
item.description:
Emotions

Reading Fiction Can Boost Your Emotional Intelligence

From Pride and Prejudice to Heated Rivalry, novels can improve emotion skills.

Posted August 23, 2026

Key points
  • Readers unconsciously learn about emotion as they read fiction.
  • Extended reading is important; you can't improve emotion skills with a small burst of reading.
  • All genres of fiction can improve emotion skills.
A cover of the novel Pride and Prejudice, by Jane Austen
Source: Public Domain, Wikipedia

When you curl up with a good book, you can lose yourself in another world. Reading is solitary, even antisocial, because you’re leaving your own world behind. But amazingly, reading fiction can improve your real-world social skills.

How Fiction Trains Your EQ

Many studies have found that reading fiction improves emotional intelligence, the ability to recognize and interpret the emotions of others from their facial expressions, voice, posture, and so on. Why? Fiction is full of characters’ emotions, and the experience of reading about them helps your emotional skills in the real world.

Fiction has two kinds of words that convey emotions. First, fiction contains emotion labels, like anger, disgust, and excitement. My colleagues and I found that fiction contains far more emotion labels than either speech or nonfiction writing. Second, fiction is full of words describing emotion expressions—behaviors like blush, yell, and laugh. These two types of words are key to describing how a character feels and acts in this fictional world. Readers can use these words and the broader context to infer emotional states of the characters.

Emotion labels and expressions provide a “training ground” for readers to learn about human emotions while they read. Readers aren’t deliberately memorizing emotion words; instead, they understand the story and unconsciously learn about emotions along the way. Many studies have found that people who read a lot of fiction are better able to interpret the emotions of others by observing their eyes, facial expressions, posture, or tone of voice.

Two Myths About Reading and Emotion

The idea that fiction is an emotion training ground makes sense, and it can help us dismiss harmful myths about reading and emotion.

Myth 1: You can improve your emotion skills with just one five-minute block of reading. This idea doesn’t fit with the “training ground” concept because five minutes of reading isn’t enough to train someone's emotion skills any more than five minutes of hitting a tennis ball could make them a tennis star. While people who read regularly tend to have superior emotion recognition skills, five minutes of reading doesn’t do much. Reading isn't magic; it's valuable practice for your emotional intelligence.

Myth 2: Only the “right kind” of novels will tune up your emotion skills. The myth assumes that literary fiction—novels like Pride and Prejudice, The Great Gatsby, and The Handmaid’s Tale—handles character feelings with more subtlety. They may have fewer explicit emotion labels like sad and more emotional expressions like sigh, compared with other genres. This subtlety is supposed to make readers work harder to understand what they're reading, which is supposed to be helpful for understanding emotions in the real world.

Myth #2 has two problems. First, there’s no good evidence that literary fiction is better at tuning emotion skills. Instead, studies show that reading in many genres improves emotion recognition.

The second problem with Myth #2 is that different fiction genres overlap, with novels of all types mentioning both emotion labels and emotion behaviors. I think this point is clearer with some examples. Let's look at a few sentences from two novels about characters who originally hated each other but eventually fall in love. Jane Austen’s Pride and Prejudice (1813) is a beloved example of literary fiction, and Rachel Ried’s Heated Rivalry (2019) is a bestselling modern romance novel. The books were written over 200 years apart, yet both contain many examples of emotion labels and emotion expressions:

The first two excerpts show how the main character in each book experiences mixed emotions at a turbulent time. The EMOTION LABELS are capitalized:

Pride and Prejudice: “Elizabeth, AGITATED and CONFUSED, rather knew that she was HAPPY than felt herself to be so.” (Context: Elizabeth has received very good news, but she can’t relax yet. She is still dreading several difficult situations she’ll need to deal with.)

This logo is for the TV show; the book cover is not shown because it is protected by copyright
Source: Public Domain Wikipedia Commons

Heated Rivalry: “Shane had been sick with JEALOUSY, but he had also been undeniably PROUD when he'd watched Ilya Rozanov lift the cup over his head and roar.” (Context: Shane, whose team did not advance to the Stanley Cup Finals, watches his rival Ilya and his team celebrate winning the Stanley Cup on TV.)

The next two examples focus on EMOTION EXPRESSIONS (capitalized here). Both excerpts show embarrassment via the characters' blushing.

Pride and Prejudice: “Their eyes instantly met, and the cheeks of both were overspread with the deepest BLUSH.” (Context: Elizabeth and Darcy unexpectedly run into each other in the company of several people who don’t know their awkward backstory.)

Heated Rivalry. “Shane BLUSHED furiously, which made Rozanov LAUGH more.” (Context: Ilya teases Shane.)

These examples show that both literary fiction and other genres contain emotion labels and emotion expressions. It's therefore not surprising that reading many fiction genres improves our emotion recognition skills. Every book has a unique mix of emotion descriptions; this variety makes reading fun and helps grow your emotional skills. So find books you enjoy, in any genre, and read them!

item.title: Does Chess Make You Smarter? What Chess Can Teach Us
item.description:
Self-Help

Does Chess Make You Smarter? What Chess Can Teach Us

Chess can show us how we make decisions, handle mistakes, and adapt.

Posted August 23, 2026

Key points
  • Chess skill is linked to several cognitive abilities, but this does not prove chess makes us smarter.
  • Chess instruction may improve some academic skills, but studies have important methodological limits.
  • Playing chess can expose habits like rushed decisions, overconfidence, and stubbornness.
Source: Arash Emamzadeh

When I was a kid in Iran, much of my time was spent studying. Whatever free time I had, I spent it reading or playing games. Tag, hide-and-seek, Lego, soccer, card games—you name it, we played it.

Perhaps the least popular game we played was chess. Why? Because it involved no physical activity, could only be played by two people, and the general consensus was that it bored everybody else to death.

I think the boredom came from how difficult chess was to understand. Unlike soccer or tag, the point of what happens on a chessboard is not always obvious until several moves later.

After all, although learning the rules of chess is relatively easy, understanding the game enough to play well can be quite hard. You need to anticipate your opponent’s moves, consider possible responses, examine different lines of play and their consequences, evaluate the resulting positions, and then choose the best move.

But does being good at chess mean you're smart? And does playing chess make you smarter?

Does chess make you smarter?

There is good evidence that chess skill is associated with a number of cognitive abilities. A large meta-analysis found that chess skill was modestly related to abilities like fluid reasoning, short-term memory, and numerical ability. In other words, people who were better at chess tended to perform better on some cognitive tests.

But this does not mean playing chess increases intelligence. For instance, someone who is good at chess may already have a higher IQ to begin with.

To investigate causality, researchers have conducted studies in which children receive chess instruction regularly and are then tested on cognitive abilities and performance in subjects such as reading and mathematics.

A meta-analysis of 24 studies found some benefits associated with chess instruction, particularly in mathematics. But the studies had important limitations, making it difficult to tell how much of those benefits came from chess itself.

In short, we still don't have strong evidence that playing chess makes people more intelligent or raises their IQ.

But there is another way to think about the value of chess. Even if skills learned in chess do not transfer directly to other areas, the game requires us to repeatedly practice cognitive skills like paying attention to details and making decisions under uncertainty.

On a personal level, I have found another potential benefit of playing chess: it kept exposing my own bad habits. The more I played, the more I noticed that the same patterns showed up in my life.

So let me tell you a little about them.

What chess has taught me about life

  1. Think ahead—but expect to be surprised

Chess rewards thinking ahead, but it also teaches that predictions can fail spectacularly. As a result, players learn to anticipate multiple ways their opponent might respond. Life is, of course, even less predictable, and our plans are disrupted all the time (my own computer froze halfway through writing this article and my file just disappeared!). So, in order to prepare for the inevitable obstacles, having backup plans isn't just smart; it's essential.

  1. Don't underestimate the little things

In chess, the pawns are the least powerful pieces, yet pawn structures can decide games. Similarly, a little time spent exercising, meditating, or reading may not seem significant on a particular day, but repeated over time, healthy habits can build a strong foundation for a better life.

  1. Every choice has a cost

Chess teaches you that a move that strengthens some squares can weaken others. In life, too, every choice opens some doors and closes others. Time spent working is time that cannot also be spent with family, for instance. Therefore, it is useful to think carefully about the tradeoffs with every major decision and ask, "Am I willing to pay the price?"

  1. Stay steady

I have lost chess games because after a blunder, I lost hope, or after an opponent’s mistake, I became overconfident. So the lesson is not to become preoccupied with either failure or success along the way to the goal. Learning to regulate our emotions can help us remain more steady.

5. Make a plan but be flexible

Winning at chess requires a plan, but the one that made sense ten moves ago may make no sense now because your opponent responded differently than expected, creating a whole new threat or opportunity. Learning to respond to those changes taught me an important lesson about resilience: I had been confusing it with stubbornness. But resilience is not about sticking with the same plan no matter what. To be resilient means recognizing when circumstances have changed and adapting our response as needed. A flexible mindset requires continually reassessing the situation as things change. Perhaps the original plan can still work with some modifications. Or maybe you need a totally new plan.

6. Think strategically, act tactically

In chess, strategy is about the larger plan, whereas tactics are about the immediate moves that turn an opportunity into an advantage. I think the same distinction can be useful in life. Strategy is putting yourself in situations where good opportunities are more likely to appear. Tactics are recognizing those opportunities and acting on them. We need both to succeed.

Takeaway

Although published research so far has found little evidence that chess makes us smarter, I feel the game still has a lot to teach us.

As an amateur chess player, I noticed that the game brought me face-to-face with the same weaknesses I struggled with in real life: rushed decisions, discouragement after mistakes, overconfidence after success, and a tendency to stick with plans that were no longer feasible.

Chess taught me that sometimes the best thing we can do is step away from our preoccupation with past mistakes and fantasies of future success, see the position we are in with clear eyes, and assess it honestly.

And then, make a move.
